title: Double treble in depth
subtitle: UK dtr — lace, fans, and tall stitch construction
excerpt: The double treble (UK dtr, US tr) starts with two yarn overs and works off the hook in three steps. It is the stitch behind most lace, fan, and long-stitch patterns, and understanding its construction demystifies every taller stitch in the family.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 3 and 4. Double treble as a lace stitch.
heroPrompt: A swatch of double treble crochet in cream cotton showing the tall, open columns, natural background, with a 4 mm hook resting alongside.

glossaryTerms.definition: A tall crochet stitch made with two initial yarn overs, worked off the hook in three pairs. UK double treble equals US treble (tr). Taller than a treble; used in lace, fans, and extended-height pattern stitches.

content.text: starts where the treble ends: two initial yarn overs, four loops on the hook after inserting, and three "work off two" steps to finish. Once the treble is solid, the double treble is the same logic extended by one more pair.
Yarn over twice (two wraps around the hook) before inserting.
Insert the hook under both top loops of the next stitch.
Yarn over and pull through the stitch. Four loops on the hook.
Yarn over, pull through the first two loops. Three loops remain.
Yarn over, pull through two loops. Two loops remain.
Yarn over, pull through the final two loops. One loop. The double treble is complete.

attrs.title: The pattern for tall stitches
attrs.body: Every taller stitch adds one more initial yarn over and one more pull-through step. Treble: 1 yarn over, 2 steps. Double treble: 2 yarn overs, 3 steps. Triple treble: 3 yarn overs, 4 steps. Once you understand the pattern, any tall stitch follows.

content.text: A double treble requires a ch-4 turning chain, which counts as the first dtr of the row. Skip the first stitch at the base. At the end of the return row, work the last dtr into the top of the ch-4 turning chain from the previous row.

Double trebles appear in lace patterns where the tall height creates open airy columns, in fan stitch variations where the extra height adds drama to the fan shape, and in crossed double treble stitches where the tall crossing arm needs space to travel. They are also the stitch behind Solomon's knot (worked into very loose chain spaces) and certain Irish crochet motif petals.

attrs.heading: Double treble problems
attrs.intro: Three issues specific to the double treble.

items.symptom: The stitch collapses — the top loops fall sideways
items.cause: The initial yarn overs were worked too loosely and they unravelled during the insertion.
items.fix: Hold the two yarn overs firmly against the hook shaft during insertion. A slight finger pressure on the yarn overs before pulling through the stitch keeps them in order.

items.symptom: Lost count of how many pull-through steps were taken
items.cause: Working too fast without counting the loops remaining.
items.fix: Count the loops on the hook before each pull-through: 4, then 3, then 2, then 1. Counting aloud prevents losing track.

items.symptom: The turning chain stands noticeably taller than the first worked stitch
items.cause: The chain-4 turning chain was worked at a looser tension than the body stitches.
items.fix: Work the turning chain firmly. Some makers work ch-4 but drop to ch-3 after the first stitch to test what matches their tension.

content.text: The crossed double treble is the natural next step: two double trebles worked in reverse order so they cross in front of each other. The triple treble extends the pattern one step further (three initial yarn overs, four pull-through steps). Both appear in the Stitches tutorials in this library.
